Exploratory Data Analysis: Avalanche Danger Levels in Tyrol¶

Project: Data Analysis Project, Foundations of Data Engineering and Analytics Authors: Dominik Glätzle, Malte Braig Milestone: Exploratory data analysis (due 24/11/2026)

Research question: How accurately can the avalanche warning level issued by LWD Tirol be predicted from weather and snow data of the preceding days, and which factors (temperature, wind, precipitation, snow depth) are key to this prediction?

This notebook explores data/final.csv, the output of preprocessing.ipynb (9 regions, 2019/20–2025/26, one row per region-day; see docs/datasheet.md). The EDA is organised around the questions the modelling step needs answered:

# Section Question for modelling
1 Overview & data quality Is the table complete and consistent, or do we need to go back to preprocessing?
2 Univariate analysis What does the target look like (imbalance, ordinality)? How are the features distributed (skew, units, station effects)?
3 Bivariate analysis Which features separate the danger levels, and over which time window? Which features are redundant?
4 Multivariate analysis Do features interact? How much structure is there in the joint feature space? How strongly are rows dependent in time and space?
5 Summary What changes to preprocessing, which engineered features, which models, splits and metrics follow from this?

Only pandas, numpy and matplotlib are used (the project's existing dependencies). Spearman correlations are computed as Pearson correlations on ranks, and mutual information is estimated with quantile binning, so no extra packages are needed.

In [1]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap, BoundaryNorm
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter

pd.set_option("display.precision", 2)
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)

# Same visual language as exploration.ipynb: danger levels 1-4 as one ordered blue ramp
LEVELS = [1, 2, 3, 4]
LEVEL_COLORS = {1: "#86b6ef", 2: "#3987e5", 3: "#1c5cab", 4: "#0d366b"}
LEVEL_NAMES = {1: "1 low", 2: "2 moderate", 3: "3 considerable", 4: "4 high"}
BLUE, ORANGE, GREY = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#8a8984"

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": "#e4e3df", "grid.linewidth": 0.8, "axes.axisbelow": True,
    "axes.edgecolor": GREY, "axes.labelcolor": "#52514e", "xtick.color": "#52514e",
    "ytick.color": "#52514e", "axes.titleweight": "bold", "axes.titlesize": 11,
})


def spearman(a, b):
    # Spearman rank correlation without scipy (pairwise complete observations)
    m = a.notna() & b.notna()
    return a[m].rank().corr(b[m].rank())


def level_boxplot(ax, df, col, title=None):
    # Boxplot of one numeric column per danger level (outliers hidden, whiskers 1.5 IQR)
    groups = [df.loc[df["danger_max"] == l, col].dropna() for l in LEVELS]
    bp = ax.boxplot(groups, tick_labels=LEVELS, widths=0.6, patch_artist=True, showfliers=False,
                    medianprops={"color": "white", "linewidth": 1.5},
                    whiskerprops={"color": GREY}, capprops={"color": GREY})
    for patch, l in zip(bp["boxes"], LEVELS):
        patch.set(facecolor=LEVEL_COLORS[l], edgecolor="none")
    ax.set_title(title or col, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("danger level", fontsize=8)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)


def stacked_share(ax, table, title):
    # Horizontal 100 % stacked bars of the danger level share per row of `table`
    share = table.div(table.sum(axis=1), axis=0)
    left = np.zeros(len(share))
    for level in share.columns:
        ax.barh(share.index.astype(str), share[level], left=left, color=LEVEL_COLORS[level],
                label=LEVEL_NAMES[level], height=0.7, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1)
        left += share[level].values
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1))
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.invert_yaxis()

Observations

  • All 11 weather features are complete (0 missing): the IDW station-to-region assignment in combine_stations_and_avalanche.py fills gaps from neighbouring stations, so no imputation is needed for modelling.
  • The only real gaps are in bulletin columns: danger_below (72 rows) and tendency (13 rows). The target danger_max is complete.
  • (region, date) is a unique key, so the preprocessing deduplication worked.

1.2 Temporal coverage¶

Rows only exist during the winter season. This matters for every lag or rolling feature: a naive diff() or rolling() per region would cross from the end of one season (May) to the start of the next one (Nov/Dec).

In [4]:

print("gaps between consecutive rows of a region (days):")
print(gap.value_counts().sort_index().rename_axis("gap_days").to_frame("count").T)

coverage = data.groupby("season").agg(first=("date", "min"), last=("date", "max"),
                                       days=("date", "nunique"), rows=("date", "size"))
coverage["rows_per_day"] = coverage["rows"] / coverage["days"]

Within a season the series are gap-free (every gap is exactly 1 day) and all 9 regions are present on every day. The only gaps are the ~200-day summer breaks. Consequence: all lag and rolling features must be computed per (region, season), never just per region.

1.3 A new data-quality issue: snow-depth spikes¶

snow_depth_cm is the only "state" variable in the data (all others describe the last 24 h), so its day-to-day change is the natural proxy for fresh snow and settling. Looking at that change reveals implausible one-day jumps.

In [5]:
data["snow_diff_1d_naive"] = data.groupby("region")["snow_depth_cm"].diff()              # crosses seasons
data["snow_diff_1d"] = data.groupby(["region", "season"])["snow_depth_cm"].diff()        # within season

big_naive = (data["snow_diff_1d_naive"].abs() > 60).sum()
big_within = (data["snow_diff_1d"].abs() > 60).sum()
print(f"|1-day snow depth change| > 60 cm: {big_naive} rows when computed per region, "
      f"{big_within} rows when computed per (region, season)")

# A "spike" = a big jump that is (mostly) reversed on the next day
nxt = data.groupby(["region", "season"])["snow_diff_1d"].shift(-1)
spike = (data["snow_diff_1d"].abs() > 50) & (nxt.abs() > 50) & (np.sign(data["snow_diff_1d"]) != np.sign(nxt))
data["snow_spike"] = spike
print("\nsuspected sensor spikes (jump > 50 cm that reverses the next day):")
data.loc[spike, ["region", "station_name", "date", "snow_depth_cm", "snow_diff_1d"]].assign(next_day_diff=nxt[spike])

In [6]:
examples = data.loc[spike, ["region", "season"]].drop_duplicates().head(3)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(examples), figsize=(13, 3.2))
for ax, (_, ex) in zip(axes, examples.iterrows()):
    s = data[(data["region"] == ex["region"]) & (data["season"] == ex["season"])].set_index("date")
    causal = s["snow_depth_cm"].rolling(3, min_periods=1).median()
    ax.plot(s.index, s["snow_depth_cm"], color=GREY, lw=1, label="raw")
    ax.plot(s.index, causal, color=BLUE, lw=1.6, label="rolling median (last 3 days)")
    ax.scatter(s.index[s["snow_spike"]], s.loc[s["snow_spike"], "snow_depth_cm"], color=ORANGE, zorder=3,
               s=25, label="flagged spike")
    ax.set_title(f"{s['station_name'].iloc[0]} ({ex['season']})", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_ylabel("snow depth (cm)")
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=30, labelsize=7)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
  • Most of the very large "jumps" are not errors but artifacts of differencing across the summer gap. They disappear when grouping by season.
  • Among the remaining ones are single-day sensor spikes: snow depth rises or drops by 50–145 cm and returns the next day, which is physically impossible. (A few other jumps last 2 days, e.g. Valluga/Galtür in early Dec 2020, so the 1-day rule is a conservative lower bound.) Several neighbouring regions show the same spike on the same day because they share stations through the IDW assignment.
  • A causal rolling median over the last 3 days removes them. It only uses past values, so it adds no leakage. A centred filter would use day d+1 and must not be used for features.

Back to preprocessing: we will add this despiking step (and the per-season grouping) to the feature pipeline before computing any snow-depth difference features.

In [7]:
data["snow_depth_clean"] = (data.groupby(["region", "season"])["snow_depth_cm"]
                                .transform(lambda x: x.rolling(3, min_periods=1).median()))
data = data.drop(columns="snow_diff_1d_naive")

mean danger by days_before: {0: 2.62, 1: 2.21}
  • danger_max is consistent with its components, and in 89% of rows it equals danger_above. The elevation split matters for the lower level, not for the maximum, so danger_max is a sensible target.
  • danger_am != danger_pm on ~10% of days. These are mostly spring days with a daytime wet-snow increase.
  • Bulletins published on the morning of the valid day (days_before = 0) have clearly higher danger. These are mostly updates during critical situations. days_before is only known once the bulletin is published, so it cannot be used as a feature. It also means that for these rows forecasters had ~12 h more information than our 24 h window (which ends at 17:00 on d-1), which caps achievable accuracy for exactly the high-danger days.
  • danger_below, danger_am, danger_pm, elev_limit, problems and tendency of the same bulletin are part of the label and must not be used as features. Only their previous-day values are available at prediction time.

level-4 share per season:
season     2019/20  2020/21  2021/22  2022/23  2023/24  2024/25  2025/26
% level 4      4.4      6.4      5.5      2.8      2.9      1.2      6.5
  • Strong imbalance: level 2 alone is half of the data, level 4 is ~4%, level 5 never occurs. A majority-class model already reaches ~51% accuracy, so accuracy alone is misleading. We will report macro-F1, per-class recall and a confusion matrix, and consider class weights.
  • The target is ordinal: predicting 3 for a true 4 is less wrong than predicting 1. Next to the classification metrics we will report "within ±1 level" accuracy and mean absolute error, and try an ordinal formulation (e.g. regression with rounding, or cumulative binary models P(level > k)).
  • Seasonality: danger peaks in Dec–Feb and level 1 dominates in spring/early winter. Since the snowpack history drives this, a calendar feature (day of season / month) is a cheap proxy.
  • Seasons differ a lot. The share of level-4 days varies several-fold between winters. A season-based test split (latest winter) is therefore a real distribution shift, and we will also evaluate with leave-one-season-out cross-validation to see the variance.
  • Regions are similar, except Kitzbüheler Alpen (Hahnenkamm), which is lower and has more than twice as many level-1 days. A region identifier (or station elevation) should be a feature.

number of problems per bulletin: {0: 642, 1: 3244, 2: 4791, 3: 1035, 4: 17}

wind_slab and persistent_weak_layers dominate. Persistent weak layers are a property of the snowpack history (e.g. a cold, low-snow early winter), so they cannot be explained by the last few days of weather. This hints that long-window features (snow depth and temperature since the start of the season) will matter, not just short-term loading.

Observations and consequences

  • Precipitation is extremely right-skewed (skew > 5, about half of all days dry). Use log-transformed or accumulated values for linear models; trees are unaffected.
  • Sunshine has a spike at 0 (overcast or snowing). Its information overlaps with precipitation and humidity (see 3.3).
  • Wind direction is circular. The raw degree value is meaningless for any model (0° ≈ 360°), so encode it as sin / cos, ideally weighted by wind speed. The dominant directions are W–NW (storm/loading directions) and S (föhn).
  • Pressure is station-level and not reduced to sea level. Its distribution is a mix of one bump per station elevation (from ~705 hPa at Pitztaler Gletscher to ~847 hPa at Schmirn), so the raw value mostly identifies the station. Only the anomaly per station (deviation from the station mean, or the 24/72 h tendency) carries weather information.
  • The same station effect applies, more weakly, to temperature and snow depth: the median snow depth ranges from ~41 cm (Schmirn) to ~161 cm (Pitztaler Gletscher), but the danger level distribution is almost the same in these regions (see 2.1). Absolute snow depth therefore says more about the station than the danger. We will add per-station standardised versions (z-scores computed on the training seasons only) next to the raw values.

  • Precipitation, humidity and wind gusts increase monotonically with the level, and sunshine decreases. This is the classic "snowfall + wind = loading" signal.
  • Temperature decreases with the level (median mean temp −1.5 °C at level 1 vs. −4.7 °C at level 4): cold days go with storms, new snow and wind slabs. The link is weaker than for precipitation, though, because in spring warm days drive wet-snow danger in the opposite direction. This is an interaction with season/month (see 4.1).
  • Snow depth is higher for levels 3–4 but the boxes overlap a lot, partly due to the station effect from 2.3.
  • No single feature separates the levels cleanly. Levels 2 and 3 in particular overlap in every feature, so we expect most errors between these two classes.

3.2 Which time window matters? (key input for feature engineering)¶

The bulletin summarises the last several days of loading, not just the last 24 hours. We test this directly: Spearman correlation between danger_max and (a) lagged daily values and (b) rolling aggregates over different window lengths, computed per (region, season).

In [17]:
grp = data.groupby(["region", "season"])
y = data["danger_max"]

lag_corr = pd.DataFrame({
    f"{col}": [spearman(grp[col].shift(lag), y) for lag in range(8)]
    for col in ["precip_sum_mm", "wind_gust_max", "rel_humidity_mean", "sunshine_sum", "air_temp_mean"]
}, index=pd.Index(range(8), name="lag (days)"))

windows = [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 14, 21]
win_corr = pd.DataFrame({
    "precip sum": [spearman(grp["precip_sum_mm"].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(w, min_periods=1).sum()), y) for w in windows],
    "max gust": [spearman(grp["wind_gust_max"].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(w, min_periods=1).max()), y) for w in windows],
    "snow depth change (despiked)": [spearman(grp["snow_depth_clean"].diff(w), y) for w in windows],
    "mean air temp": [spearman(grp["air_temp_mean"].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(w, min_periods=1).mean()), y) for w in windows],
}, index=pd.Index(windows, name="window (days)"))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.8))
for col in lag_corr:
    axes[0].plot(lag_corr.index, lag_corr[col], marker="o", ms=4, label=col)
axes[0].axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("lag (days before the 24 h window)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Spearman ρ with danger_max")
axes[0].set_title("Single lagged days")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)
for col in win_corr:
    axes[1].plot(win_corr.index, win_corr[col], marker="o", ms=4, label=col)
axes[1].axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)

precip sum max gust snow depth change (despiked) mean air temp
window (days)
1 0.36 0.26 0.16 -0.14
2 0.41 0.28 0.14 -0.14
3 0.42 0.29 0.16 -0.14
5 0.42 0.30 0.20 -0.14
7 0.42 0.28 0.22 -0.15
10 0.39 0.23 0.24 -0.18
14 0.35 0.17 0.30 -0.23
21 0.27 0.12 0.34 -0.27
  • The signal of a single day of precipitation fades slowly: day d-1 still has ρ ≈ 0.33 and even a week back it is still positive. Danger has memory.
  • Accumulated precipitation is clearly stronger than the last day alone (ρ ≈ 0.36 → 0.42) and plateaus at 3–7 days (ρ ≈ 0.42), the typical length of a storm cycle.
  • The max gust over 3–5 days is better than the last day's gust.
  • The snow depth change gets more informative with longer windows (ρ 0.16 at 1–3 days → 0.34 at 21 days). It captures the build-up of the snowpack over whole storm periods.
  • The mean temperature also becomes more informative over longer windows (ρ −0.14 → −0.27): long cold spells go with higher danger, which fits persistent weak layers forming in cold, shallow snowpacks.
  • Consequence for feature engineering: besides the 24 h values, build rolling features with 3, 7 and 14 day windows (precip sums, max gusts, snow depth changes on the despiked series, temperature means), plus 1–2 day lags. All of them are computed per (region, season) and use only data before the cutoff.

3.3 Feature–target correlation and redundancy between features¶

In [18]:
f = data.copy()
g = f.groupby(["region", "season"])
f["precip_3d"] = g["precip_sum_mm"].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(3, min_periods=1).sum())
f["precip_7d"] = g["precip_sum_mm"].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(7, min_periods=1).sum())
f["gust_max_3d"] = g["wind_gust_max"].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(3, min_periods=1).max())
f["snow_change_3d"] = g["snow_depth_clean"].diff(3)
f["snow_change_14d"] = g["snow_depth_clean"].diff(14)
f["temp_mean_3d"] = g["air_temp_mean"].transform(lambda x: x.rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean())
f["temp_range"] = f["air_temp_max"] - f["air_temp_min"]
f["pressure_anom"] = f["pressure_mean"] - f.groupby("station_name")["pressure_mean"].transform("mean")
f["snow_depth_z"] = (f["snow_depth_cm"] - f.groupby("station_name")["snow_depth_cm"].transform("mean")) \
                    / f.groupby("station_name")["snow_depth_cm"].transform("std")
f["day_of_season"] = (f["date"] - f.groupby(["region", "season"])["date"].transform("min")).dt.days
f["wind_sin"] = np.sin(np.deg2rad(f["wind_dir_deg"]))
f["wind_cos"] = np.cos(np.deg2rad(f["wind_dir_deg"]))

1 air_temp_mean air_temp_min 0.97

  • The strongest single predictors are the multi-day precipitation sums (ρ ≈ 0.42), followed by the 14-day snow-depth change, gusts (3-day max), humidity and sunshine (negative). These are mostly engineered features, which confirms 3.2.
  • pressure_anom correlates negatively with danger (low pressure = storm), whereas the raw pressure_mean is almost uninformative. This confirms that the raw value mostly encodes the station.
  • Redundancy: the three temperatures (mean/min/max, ρ > 0.9), and wind_speed_mean / wind_gust_max are highly correlated (ρ > 0.75), and the different windows of the same variable overlap as well. Tree ensembles cope with this, but for the (multinomial/ordinal) logistic regression baseline we should keep one representative per group (e.g. air_temp_mean + temp_range, wind_gust_max, precip_3d + precip_7d) and standardise, otherwise the coefficients are unstable and cannot be interpreted. For the "which factors matter" part of the research question, we will use permutation importance on groups of correlated features, because importance gets split between correlated features.
  • Correlation does not mean direction-independent effects: temperature is close to zero overall but matters conditionally (next section).

3.4 Categorical features vs. target: what is known from yesterday's bulletin?¶

The previous day's bulletin is published before the prediction cutoff, so its level, tendency and problems are legitimate features.

precip_3d gust_max_3d air_temp_max snow_change_14d month
problem

  • Persistence is a very strong baseline: ~79% of days keep yesterday's level, vs. 51% for the majority class. Any weather model has to be compared to it. More importantly, the interesting (and safety-relevant) part of the task is predicting the changes.
  • Yesterday's tendency is informative: after "increasing" the level rises on about half of the days, after "decreasing" it falls in ~40%, after "steady" it stays the same in ~86%. It is an expert forecast of exactly what we want to predict, so it is a strong but "cheating-adjacent" feature. We will train models with and without bulletin history (prev_danger, prev_tendency, previous problems) to separate the weather signal (the research question) from forecaster inertia.
  • Problems map to weather regimes: new_snow goes with high 3-day precipitation and the highest danger (85% of these days are level 3–4), wind_slab with strong gusts, wet_snow / gliding_snow with warm max temperatures in spring. This supports the idea that different weather combinations lead to the same danger level, i.e. non-linear models. Previous-day problems are a useful categorical feature (multi-hot encoding).

4. Multivariate analysis¶

4.1 Interactions: precipitation × temperature and precipitation × wind¶

In [22]:
def mean_level_grid(ax, df, xcol, ycol, xbins, ybins, xlabel, ylabel, title, min_n=30):
    xb = pd.cut(df[xcol], xbins)
    yb = pd.cut(df[ycol], ybins)
    tab = df.groupby([yb, xb], observed=False)["danger_max"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    m = tab["mean"].unstack().where(tab["size"].unstack() >= min_n)
    n = tab["size"].unstack()
    im = ax.imshow(m.values, cmap="Blues", vmin=1.5, vmax=3.5, origin="lower", aspect="auto")
    ax.set_xticks(range(m.shape[1]), [str(i) for i in m.columns], rotation=35, ha="right", fontsize=7)
    ax.set_yticks(range(m.shape[0]), [str(i) for i in m.index], fontsize=7)
    for i in range(m.shape[0]):
        for j in range(m.shape[1]):
            if not np.isnan(m.values[i, j]):
                ax.text(j, i, f"{m.values[i, j]:.1f}\nn={n.values[i, j]}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6,
                        color="white" if m.values[i, j] > 2.7 else "#0b0b0b")
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_ylabel(ylabel); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10); ax.grid(False)
    return im

pbins = [-0.01, 1, 5, 15, 30, 200]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.6), layout="constrained")
mean_level_grid(axes[0], f, "precip_3d", "air_temp_mean", pbins, [-30, -10, -5, 0, 5, 20],
                "precipitation last 3 days (mm)", "mean air temp (°C)", "Precip × temperature")
mean_level_grid(axes[1], f, "precip_3d", "gust_max_3d", pbins, [0, 10, 15, 20, 25, 60],
                "precipitation last 3 days (mm)", "max gust last 3 days (m/s)", "Precip × wind")
f["season_month"] = (f["month"] - 8) % 12  # Nov=3, Dec=4, Jan=5, ..., May=9 (monotone over a winter)
im = mean_level_grid(axes[2], f, "air_temp_max", "season_month", [-30, -5, 0, 5, 10, 25], [2.5, 4.5, 5.5, 6.5, 7.5, 9.5],
                     "max air temp (°C)", "", "Temperature × month")
axes[2].set_yticks(range(5), ["Nov–Dec", "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr–May"])
fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="mean danger level")
Out[22]:
<matplotlib.colorbar.Colorbar at 0x77ef049263c0>

(Cells with fewer than 30 region-days are left empty.)

  • Precip × wind: precipitation dominates (mean level ~1.9 → ~3.2 from dry to > 30 mm). Wind adds the most on days with little precipitation (dry days: 1.9 at calm vs. 2.5 at gusts > 25 m/s, i.e. wind transport of old snow). With heavy precipitation the level is already high and wind adds little. The effects are not additive.
  • Precip × temperature: with heavy precipitation, cold is more dangerous (≈ 3.3 at < −5 °C vs. ≈ 2.8 at 0–5 °C: light, poorly bonded new snow). Without precipitation, the warmest days are slightly more dangerous (wet snow).
  • Temperature × month: in Nov–Feb, colder days are clearly more dangerous (≈ 2.8 below −5 °C vs. ≈ 1.9–2.2 above 5 °C). In March–May this effect disappears and the warmest days (> 10 °C) are slightly more dangerous again (wet snow, gliding snow). The temperature effect thus depends on the season, which a linear model with one additive temperature term cannot express. We will use tree ensembles and/or add explicit interactions (temperature × spring indicator, positive degree-sum over the last days).

4.2 Joint structure: PCA of the engineered feature space¶

In [23]:
PCA_COLS = ["precip_3d", "precip_7d", "gust_max_3d", "snow_change_3d", "snow_change_14d", "temp_mean_3d",
            "temp_range", "pressure_anom", "snow_depth_z", "rel_humidity_mean", "sunshine_sum",
            "wind_speed_mean", "day_of_season"]
X = f[PCA_COLS].copy()
X["precip_3d"] = np.log1p(X["precip_3d"]); X["precip_7d"] = np.log1p(X["precip_7d"])
mask = X.notna().all(axis=1)
Xs = (X[mask] - X[mask].mean()) / X[mask].std()

U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xs.values, full_matrices=False)
explained = S**2 / (S**2).sum()
scores = Xs.values @ Vt[:2].T
lv = f.loc[mask, "danger_max"].values

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [0.8, 1.2, 1]})
axes[0].bar(range(1, len(explained) + 1), explained, color=BLUE)
axes[0].plot(range(1, len(explained) + 1), explained.cumsum(), color=ORANGE, marker="o", ms=3)
axes[0].set_xlabel("component"); axes[0].set_title("Explained variance (bars) and cumulative")
axes[0].yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1)); axes[0].grid(axis="x", visible=False)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
order = rng.permutation(len(lv))
axes[1].scatter(scores[order, 0], scores[order, 1], c=[LEVEL_COLORS[l] for l in lv[order]], s=4, alpha=0.6, lw=0)
for l in LEVELS:
    cx, cy = scores[lv == l, 0].mean(), scores[lv == l, 1].mean()
    axes[1].scatter(cx, cy, color=LEVEL_COLORS[l], s=120, edgecolor="black", lw=1, zorder=3, label=f"centroid {LEVEL_NAMES[l]}")
axes[1].set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({explained[0]:.0%})"); axes[1].set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({explained[1]:.0%})")
axes[1].set_title("Region-days in PC1/PC2, coloured by danger level")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False, loc="best")

load = pd.DataFrame(Vt[:2].T, index=PCA_COLS, columns=["PC1", "PC2"])
ld = load.reindex(load["PC1"].abs().sort_values().index)
yy = np.arange(len(ld))
axes[2].barh(yy - 0.2, ld["PC1"], height=0.4, color=BLUE, label="PC1")
axes[2].barh(yy + 0.2, ld["PC2"], height=0.4, color=ORANGE, label="PC2")
axes[2].set_yticks(yy, ld.index, fontsize=7); axes[2].axvline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)

print("mean PC1 per level:", {l: round(scores[lv == l, 0].mean(), 2) for l in LEVELS})

mean PC1 per level: {1: np.float64(1.25), 2: np.float64(0.36), 3: np.float64(-0.84), 4: np.float64(-2.91)}
  • The first component is a "storm" axis (precipitation, humidity, low sunshine, low pressure anomaly, rising snow depth), and the level centroids are ordered monotonically along it (level 1 → 4). The sign of a principal component is arbitrary, here the storm direction is negative. This is a good sign that a monotone/ordinal relationship exists.
  • Variance is spread over many components (PC1 ≈ 29%, PC1+PC2 ≈ 43%), so the features are not just one dimension. Dimensionality reduction before modelling is not needed: the feature set is small and the components are not much more interpretable than the features.
  • The classes overlap heavily in the 2-D projection, especially 2 vs. 3. Weather alone will give a noisy separation, which matches the concept's expectation (point stations, expert label). Realistically we can expect macro-F1 well below the persistence accuracy unless bulletin history is used.

4.3 How much information does each feature carry? (mutual information)¶

Spearman correlation only measures monotone relationships. Mutual information (MI) also captures non-monotone ones (e.g. temperature). We estimate it by binning each feature into 10 quantile bins.

In [24]:
def mutual_info(x, y, bins=10):
    m = x.notna() & y.notna()
    xb = pd.qcut(x[m].rank(method="first"), bins, labels=False)
    p = pd.crosstab(xb, y[m], normalize=True).values
    px, py = p.sum(1, keepdims=True), p.sum(0, keepdims=True)
    nz = p > 0
    return (p[nz] * np.log2(p[nz] / (px @ py)[nz])).sum()

H = -(f["danger_max"].value_counts(normalize=True) * np.log2(f["danger_max"].value_counts(normalize=True))).sum()
feat_mi = ["prev_danger"] + RAW + ENG
mi = pd.Series({c: mutual_info(f[c], f["danger_max"]) for c in feat_mi}).sort_values()
rho = pd.Series({c: spearman(f[c], f["danger_max"]) for c in feat_mi})

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 7))
ax.barh(mi.index, mi.values, color=[ORANGE if c == "prev_danger" else BLUE for c in mi.index], height=0.65)
for i, v in enumerate(mi.values):
    ax.text(v + 0.003, i, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=7, color="#52514e")
ax.set_xlabel(f"mutual information with danger_max (bits; target entropy = {H:.2f} bits)")
ax.set_title("Information per feature (orange: yesterday's level)")
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout()

pd.DataFrame({"MI_bits": mi, "spearman": rho}).sort_values("MI_bits", ascending=False).head(10)
Out[24]:
MI_bits spearman
prev_danger 0.61 0.80
precip_3d 0.16 0.42
precip_7d 0.15 0.42
precip_sum_mm 0.12 0.36
snow_change_14d 0.12 0.31
snow_change_3d 0.09 0.16
sunshine_sum 0.08 -0.28

  • Yesterday's level alone carries far more information than any weather feature. This is the quantitative version of the persistence finding.
  • Among the weather features, the ranking mostly matches the correlations (multi-day precipitation, 14-day snow change, sunshine, gusts, humidity). But day_of_season (ρ only −0.10, yet MI in the top group) and the short-term snow_change_3d rank much higher by MI. They have non-monotone effects (danger is highest mid-season; both strong settling and strong gain matter) that the correlation misses.
  • Every single weather feature explains only a small part of the ~1.6-bit target entropy. The prediction has to come from combining many weak signals, which favours ensembles (random forest, gradient boosting).

4.4 Dependence between rows (time and space)¶

Rows are not independent: the level is autocorrelated over days, and neighbouring regions share weather (and partly stations through IDW). This decides how we split train and test data.

In [25]:
# Temporal: autocorrelation of danger_max within (region, season)
acf = [spearman(f["danger_max"], g["danger_max"].shift(k)) for k in range(1, 22)]

# Spatial: on how many days do all 9 regions have the same level? Correlation of weather between regions
daily = f.pivot(index="date", columns="region", values="danger_max")
same_all = (daily.nunique(axis=1) == 1).mean()
precip_wide = f.pivot(index="date", columns="region", values="precip_sum_mm")
region_corr = precip_wide.rank().corr()
level_corr = daily.rank().corr()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1, 1]})
axes[0].bar(range(1, 22), acf, color=BLUE)
axes[0].set_xlabel("lag (days)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Spearman ρ")
axes[0].set_title("Autocorrelation of the danger level"); axes[0].grid(axis="x", visible=False)
for ax, cm, title in [(axes[1], level_corr, "Danger level: correlation between regions"),
                      (axes[2], region_corr, "24 h precipitation: correlation between regions")]:
    im = ax.imshow(cm, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    labels = [r[-2:] for r in cm.columns]
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(labels)), labels, fontsize=7); ax.set_yticks(range(len(labels)), labels, fontsize=7)
    for i in range(len(cm)):
        for j in range(len(cm)):
            ax.text(j, i, f"{cm.iloc[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.5,
                    color="white" if cm.iloc[i, j] > 0.6 else "#0b0b0b")

fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[1:], shrink=0.8)

print(f"all 9 regions share the same level on {same_all:.1%} of days")
print(f"autocorrelation: lag 1 = {acf[0]:.2f}, lag 7 = {acf[6]:.2f}, lag 21 = {acf[20]:.2f}")

all 9 regions share the same level on 45.6% of days
autocorrelation: lag 1 = 0.80, lag 7 = 0.30, lag 21 = 0.07
  • The level is strongly autocorrelated (ρ ≈ 0.8 at lag 1, ≈ 0.3 after a week, ≈ 0 after three weeks). With a random train/test split, the test days would have their neighbouring days in the training data, and the model could learn the level by "looking up" the surrounding days. Its score would then be far too optimistic.
  • Regions are strongly correlated with each other: on 46% of days all 9 regions have the same level. This is especially true for the western regions (07, 10, 13; ρ 0.89–0.96 for the level, ≈ 0.98 for precipitation) because they share nearly the same stations through IDW. Kitzbüheler Alpen (17) is the most independent region by danger level, yet its 24 h precipitation is practically identical to Tuxer Alps West (15) and Zillertal Alps NW (23) (ρ ≈ 1.00): with k = 3 IDW the three regions effectively get their precipitation from the same station(s). A split by region would leak information in the same way.
  • Consequence: split by season: train on 2019/20–2023/24, validate on 2024/25 (hyperparameter tuning), test once on 2025/26. In addition, use leave-one-season-out cross-validation to see how much the scores vary between winters. The effective sample size is much smaller than 9,729 independent observations, so we should avoid overly complex models and interpret small differences in scores carefully.

5. Summary: what the EDA means for the next steps¶

5.1 Changes to the data processing (back to preprocessing)¶

Finding Action
One-day snow-depth spikes of ±100 cm (sensor errors, propagated to neighbouring regions by IDW) Despike snow_depth_cm with a causal 3-day rolling median before computing any snow-change feature
Naive diff/rolling per region crosses the summer gap Compute all lag/rolling features per (region, season); the first days of each season get NaN / shorter windows
pressure_mean is station-level (705–847 hPa), raw value encodes the station Replace it with a per-station anomaly and a pressure tendency
Regions 15, 17 and 23 receive practically identical precipitation (shared station through IDW, 4.4) Check the station assignment for precip_sum_mm in assign_stations_to_regions.py, add a nearer precipitation station if one exists, otherwise document it as a limitation
days_before, same-day danger_*, problems, tendency, elev_limit are part of the label Exclude them from features (leakage); only previous-day bulletin values are allowed

5.2 Feature engineering¶

  • Multi-day accumulations (strongest signal, 3.2): precipitation sums over 3/7 days, max gust over 3 days, snow-depth change over 3/7/14/21 days on the despiked series, mean temperature over 3 and 14–21 days, plus 1–2-day lags.
  • Station normalisation (2.3): per-station z-scores of snow depth/temperature, fitted on the training seasons only.
  • Encodings: wind direction as sin/cos (circular), log1p of precipitation for linear models, region one-hot / station elevation, day_of_season or month.
  • Interactions (4.1): temperature × spring (wet snow), precipitation × wind (loading). Explicitly for the linear model, implicitly for trees.
  • Bulletin history (3.4): prev_danger, prev_tendency, previous-day problems (multi-hot). These are run as a separate feature set to separate the weather signal from persistence.

5.3 Modelling and evaluation¶

  • Baselines: majority class (~51% accuracy) and persistence (~79%). The latter is the bar to beat.
  • Models: gradient boosting / random forest as the main models (many weak, interacting, partly non-monotone signals: 4.1, 4.3), (ordinal) logistic regression on a reduced, non-redundant feature set as an interpretable comparison (3.3).
  • Experiments: (a) weather features only, (b) weather + bulletin history, to answer how accurately weather alone predicts the level.
  • Split: by season (train 2019/20–2023/24, validate 2024/25, test 2025/26) + leave-one-season-out CV. No random splits, because of strong temporal and spatial dependence (4.4).
  • Metrics: macro-F1, per-class recall (especially level 4), confusion matrix, within-±1-level accuracy and MAE (ordinal target), and accuracy on days where the level changes (where persistence always fails). Class weights for the imbalance. Level 5 cannot be learned (0 rows).
  • "Which factors matter": permutation importance on groups of correlated features (precipitation group, wind group, temperature group, snow-depth group), since single-feature importances are split between correlated features (3.3).

5.4 Expectations and limitations¶

The weather signal is real but weak per feature (max |ρ| ≈ 0.42, MI ≤ 0.16 bits vs. 1.6 bits target entropy), levels 2 and 3 overlap strongly, and the label also depends on information we do not have (snowpack stratigraphy, morning updates for days_before = 0). We therefore expect a weather-only model to clearly beat the majority class, but to have a hard time beating persistence in plain accuracy. The added value has to be shown on change days and in the ordinal metrics.
